clue.text: Departs on time, followed by unending torment in England’s prime reason for delay

indicators.note: something without an ending has lost its final letter, so the word after it is cut short

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
torment is hell; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A train departs punctually, but Britain's favourite excuse for lateness soon brings misery to commuters.
explanation.walkthrough: LEAVES ON THE LINE is the notorious British railway excuse for autumn delays, when fallen leaves make rails slippery.
explanation.definitionFit: Fallen foliage on railway tracks is a famous cause of late trains in Britain every autumn.

clue.text: Clue to no few typos in excuse for delay

indicators.note: the answer itself reads as a cryptic clue whose instruction word scrambles the following letters into the phrase given

blocks.note: the first word of the answer, read as a clue, is the anagram signal

explanation.surface: A grumble that a crossword clue is riddled with misprints, offered as an excuse for being late.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read WRONG TYPE OF SNOW as a clue, and WRONG tells you to rearrange TYPE OF SNOW, giving no few typos. It is a famous 1991 British Rail excuse for snow-bound trains.
explanation.definitionFit: British Rail once blamed cancelled trains on unusually powdery flakes, and the phrase became a byword for lame railway apologies.

clue.text: One follows game’s idol, for example: as universal as contrary

indicators.note: contrary means the opposite way round, so the string of pieces is read from right to left

blocks.note: an idol is a false god
e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
U is the film-rating abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: A sports fan's hero is described as being as universal as he is contrary.
explanation.walkthrough: A sausage dog is a dachshund, bred to hunt badgers, so it follows game; the 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: The dachshund was originally a hunting breed that tracked badgers and other quarry underground.

clue.text: Supports delays

blocks.note: first meaning: ledges that hold things up

explanation.walkthrough: The same two words clue 17 down; here the answer is a plural noun for the first and a verb for the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat wall-mounted boards bear books and objects, and to put a plan aside is to postpone it.

clue.text: Boatman under duty to provide conveyance

indicators.note: in a down clue, under puts the setter's pronoun below the word for duty, so it comes second

blocks.note: Boatman is the setter, who refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: The setter complains of paying tax so a vehicle can be supplied.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter's pseudonym, so it stands for I; under places it below the duty in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab for hire is a means of transport, a vehicle carrying passengers.

clue.text: They cause delays, with fix needed: it’ll go about a long time

indicators.note: if a fix is needed the letters are broken and must be put together differently

blocks.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Things causing delays need repairing, and someone grumbles that it will take forever.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram covers only it'll go about; a long time then supplies the final four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Worldwide computer system failures halt flights, payments and trains, holding everyone up.

clue.text: Tendency for delay, caught in airport’s alarmingly British?

indicators.note: something done alarmingly is wild and disordered, so the word before it is jumbled
in places the cricket abbreviation inside the jumbled letters

blocks.note: the letters of this word, apostrophe dropped
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
British is a nationality; the question mark flags a definition by example

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether getting stuck in an airport and its terrible queues is a typically British habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitually putting things off until later is a tendency to delay tasks.

clue.text: Returning for every fish to make someone catch it?

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word for every is read backwards

blocks.note: a roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: An angler going back for each fish so that someone else can land it.
explanation.walkthrough: To catch it is an idiom for being told off; the fishing surface makes it look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: To scold or rebuke someone is to make them be on the receiving end of trouble.

clue.text: Draw Sally, purer with clothing removed

indicators.note: stripping off clothing removes the outer layer, so each word loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to sketch a girl called Sally, who would look more innocent undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Draw looks like an art instruction but is a noun: an attraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A draw is an attraction or pull, and charm that attracts people is the same thing.

clue.text: Things that happen to person in bible (New Testament) with son

blocks.note: Eve is the first woman in Genesis
s is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Musing on the things that befall a biblical figure and her son in the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Occurrences or happenings are what the plural noun means.

clue.text: Dial-A-Clue? That’s cool

indicators.note: the answer is a clue to the word before it, and its second half tells you to read the first half backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, then read backwards
the second half of the answer is the instruction word in the clue that leads to Dial

explanation.surface: An old phone service offering puzzle hints is pronounced cool.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read LAID BACK as a clue and it means 'LAID written backwards', which gives Dial.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxed and unflustered people are described as cool or easy-going.

clue.text: Does not happen to be, not even in insanity

indicators.note: rejecting the even positions leaves only the odd-numbered letters of the word

blocks.note: letters one, three, five and seven

explanation.surface: A statement that something is not, not even in a state of madness.
explanation.definitionFit: The contraction of is not means a thing lacks a quality or state.

clue.text: German rail user put out, with line taken by saboteurs?

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A German train passenger annoyed when the line is seized by wreckers.
explanation.walkthrough: With line taken adds the extra letter to the anagram fodder; the question mark admits that irregular fighters are not always saboteurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Irregular fighters often sabotage enemy supply lines, railways and bridges.

clue.text: I can be found in centre with ATM (broken) to get money sent

indicators.note: a letter found in something sits inside it, here among the jumbled letters
something broken is in pieces, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone at a town-centre cash machine that is out of order, trying to send money.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum of money transmitted to someone, often abroad, is a remittance.

clue.text: Criminal kidnaps fingerprint agents

indicators.note: criminal means crooked, so the following word's letters are bent out of shape

explanation.surface: A criminal abducts the police officers who take fingerprints.
explanation.walkthrough: Agents here means substances or means, not people: the pads supply the ink for printing fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Police take fingerprints by pressing fingers onto inked pads, which are thus the means of printing.

clue.text: Parrot heads to inner maze in the Amazon, thwarting extinction

indicators.note: the head of each word is its first letter, so only those are kept

blocks.clueFragment: inner maze in the Amazon, thwarting extinction
blocks.note: first letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A parrot is guided through an Amazon jungle labyrinth, saving its species from dying out.
explanation.walkthrough: Parrot looks like the bird of the Amazon, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to copy or repeat something mechanically, as the talking bird does.

clue.text: Supports delays

blocks.note: first meaning: bears up, keeps upright

explanation.walkthrough: The same clue as 4 down; here both halves are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb meaning to bear weight, and also to cause someone or traffic to be late.

clue.text: Report rejected from beginning to end

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the answer sounds like the words that follow

explanation.surface: A document is thrown out, perhaps over and over, from start to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: All the way through, or for the whole duration, means from start to finish.

clue.text: Slight loss of power cycling? Tea served here

indicators.note: a loss takes something away, so the word drops a letter
cycling moves round in a loop, so the first letter goes to the back

blocks.note: to slight is to spurn or snub
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A small power cut on a bike, and the question of whether tea is served here.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing P leaves SURN; moving its first letter to the end gives URNS, large tea dispensers at events.
explanation.definitionFit: Big metal vessels with taps hold hot tea at canteens and church halls.

clue.text: BBC lose tedious content in secret

indicators.note: the content of something is what it holds inside, so the answer sits within the phrase

explanation.surface: The broadcaster drops dull programming in a hush-hush move.
explanation.definitionFit: Closeted, like shut away in a private room, describes a meeting held privately.

clue.text: Boatman’s surge from bow interrupted by initial delay

indicators.note: initial means the first letter of the following word only
a word interrupted by something has it pushed into its middle

blocks.note: a bow is a tie, as in bow tie

explanation.surface: The setter, Boatman, describes a surge at the boat's bow held back by an early delay.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow suggests the front of the boat, but it is a knot: a tie. Boatman's surge is fair because a rising sea is what a boatman watches for.
explanation.definitionFit: The rising and falling of the sea is a swelling flow that sailors must reckon with.

clue.text: Expects a delay with Southern

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: A rail passenger anticipates holdups on the Southern line.
explanation.walkthrough: Southern is a rail company serving south London and the south coast, notorious for delays.
explanation.definitionFit: To await something is to look forward to it or anticipate its coming.

clue.text: Delayed often, discontented, hot and worn out

indicators.note: losing its content empties a word, leaving only its outermost letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of often
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A traveller often held up ends up unhappy, sweltering and exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Paused or postponed, as a caller left waiting on a telephone line.

clue.text: One derogated as compliant, ignoring hearts unbroken, cheerful earnest optimism

indicators.note: leaving out the hearts of words keeps just their first and last letters

explanation.surface: Describing someone scorned as a pushover, heartless to others but full of unbroken good cheer and earnest hope.
explanation.walkthrough: The insult comes from the title character of Uncle Tom's Cabin, seen as servile to white people.
explanation.definitionFit: The term is a slur for a Black person considered excessively subservient to white authority.
